Hi Sam — thanks for taking the call earlier today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment before the technical deep dive.

Key asks we heard from BroadLeaf (summary):
- Preserve request/response logs for debugging and incident investigation but ensure no PHI/PII leaves your environment.
- Trace IDs (X-Trace / X-Request-ID) must allow cross-service correlation for debugging but cannot expose user identifiers.
- Data residency: logs must remain in the US.
- Retention & deletion: default 30 days, with ability to run on-demand erasure for legal requests.
- Legal requires an auditable process for any reversible mapping.

Redwood's recommended options (high level):
1) Ingress header filtering: strip unneeded headers at the edge and explicitly allow only a small set (service, route, truncated trace token).
2) Deterministic pseudonymization: compute an HMAC-SHA256 of the incoming trace id with a customer-scoped salt and store the digest in logs (irreversible by design).
3) Reversible envelope (opt-in): if legal needs full reversibility for incident investigation, use envelope encryption (AES-GCM or AES-SIV) with keys stored in a KMS/HSM and strict access controls (audit logs + approvals).
4) Request/response body sanitization: field-level masking using a ruleset (regex + ML PII classifier) with configurable whitelist/blacklist for keys.
5) Retention & export: 30-day default retention, automated deletion job, secure export workflow (DLP scan + approval) for legal requests.

Open questions we need from BroadLeaf to finalize a POC:
- Can you share a small set of representative logs (redacted or synthetic) so we can validate our masking rules?
- Do you prefer irreversible hashing (HMAC) or an auditable reversible option for trace ids?
- Any constraints around token length (you mentioned some downstream systems expect <= 64 chars)?

Next steps proposed:

- Redwood to deliver a short tech appendix and two configuration options (HMAC-only and AES-encrypted) by Fri 9/10.
- Schedule a 60-minute engineering deep dive during week of 9/13 to validate performance and integration points (KV cache keys, batching implications, and monitoring hooks).

Attachments: redwood-traceid-hash-options.pdf (proposal), sample-pseudonymization-matrix.xlsx (config matrix).

On Mon, 6 Sep 2027 at 09:12 Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com> wrote:
> Hi Sam & Irene,
>
> Quick technical note in response to Sam's questions:
>
> - HMAC-SHA256 (customer-scoped salt): deterministic and irreversible if the salt is secret; it's useful because the same input => same digest so traces can be correlated, but original value cannot be derived from the digest. This satisfies many privacy requirements but fails the "reversible for legal" ask.
>
> - Deterministic encryption (AES-SIV or AES-GCM with associated data): reversible if we hold the decryption key. To meet legal requirements while minimizing risk we recommend:
>   * Keys stored in customer-scoped KMS (preferred) or Redwood-managed KMS with customer key wrapping.
>   * Access to decryption gated by an approval workflow (audit + sign-off) and short-lived access tokens; entire activity gets logged to the audit stream.
>
> - Practical trade-offs:
>   * Reversible approach requires careful key lifecycle management and increases operational surface (key rotation, emergency key compromise playbooks).
>   * Irreversible HMAC reduces liability surface but requires a separate forensics plan (e.g., collecting raw traces in a separate, tightly controlled store for 7 days only).
>
> - Implementation notes:
>   * Use truncated digests (e.g., first 128 bits) to keep token size small; collision risk is low with HMAC-SHA256 for our expected volume.
>   * For cross-service correlation we can use a single customer salt per account; if you need cross-region correlation, we can provision a global salt with tighter rotation windows.
>   * Masking engine: combination of regex rules + a lightweight ML PII detector — run at the ingress path to avoid storing raw PII.
>
> Proposed POC: Redwood will spin up a small transform service that ingests your sample logs, applies the chosen pseudonymization strategy, and returns a mapping of policy coverage and any gaps. Estimate: 8–12 business days once we have sample logs and a quick sync with your platform team.
>
